summary: I'll look at how earlier session summaries are written so this one matches the project's format.After the fight in Carlkin's lighthouse, the closed door is gone and only the broken floor remains. Carlkin, furious that the party opened a portal in his home without saying they still held the keystones, writes a ban on portals and teaches Gerk the rules of a Doorman: never open a door on something moving, never open one to an unknown place, and picture one exact familiar door as if opening it by hand. Gerk's aimless doorway had opened into the nothing between the arches, and the creature that nearly used the room as a birthing place was likely astral. Carlkin ties the role to the Mother's Prayer, calls Gerk a footman until he earns the rank, and explains that thirty keystones sit on ley lines: opening one functional gatehouse opens the others at once, and seating every stone in one gate would pin the gatekeepers there as dormant guardians. Over tea the party identifies their quarry as Grixto, the lich Emperor of Nyx, once the dragon rider Garixto the Betrayer, bonded to the red dragon Galixtar. They killed him twice, once after he held the Council of Nyx and again in Gilbrick, but never found the phylactery, a small mundane item that may be the helmet Walker still wears. Grixto has contacted them twice since, and he holds the Book of Vecna. Elsewhere, Walker finds Vecna waiting in a roost cave. Vecna wants that book back, admits he killed and skinned his sister Valkyrie to bind it, and offers a trade for the phylactery that Walker refuses to close. Walker takes a miniature field book and a warm red quill so he can write to Vecna later. In the cliffside ruins of the old guild, Elrus agrees that Galixtar's death could explain both the lichdom and the hunt for Al Kurin, and Walker begins to read the cave's tilted landmarks as a direction still unresolved.

plotSections.title: Aftermath in Carlkin's lighthouse
bullets: After the fight with the abyss creature, the party is in the lighthouse base, a room about forty feet across. Dana is farthest from the others. Carlkin fled upstairs and will not come down; he only leans down the stairs to talk. Benji, woken from a pile of old memorabilia, sits on a crate smoking a copper corncob pipe packed with a grass-like herb and a drop of oil. The smoke smells half sulfur and half earthy, like a coal boiler.

Gerk tries to smooth the cobbles he broke and rolls a 4. The repair looks like sandcastles, and the hole through the floor is still there. Carlkin tells him to leave it and says he will fix it later with Mending.

plotSections.title: The vanished door, the keystones, and the prophecy
bullets: Once shut, Gerk's door vanished. Nothing remains except the broken floor. Sylan calls up that the door is closed and the lower level should be safe. Carlkin answers that they nearly opened another part of hell in his lighthouse, tells them to stay away and open no more doors, and demands his desk parchment and good pen so he can write a rule while it is fresh: no portals on the premises. He does not want Gerk near the pen. The set is a well-used, high-end quill and imported ink.

Sylan takes the pen and ink upstairs. Gerk stays by the broken floor, Dana stays where she is, and Benji watches from the crate. Sylan says the four keystones are back in the party's care. Carlkin is furious: they opened a portal in his home minutes after arriving and never said they were holding the stones. He thought the job was to collect the keystones and bring them to Juten Prime.

Sylan says that delivery was finished, then an ancient prophecy made the party more important. Gerk can open doors the way he just did, they still do not really know how, and he has opened doors twice today. Carlkin asks if the prophecy is about Gerk. Sylan says it seems so: Gerk is the important one and the rest are along for the ride. Dana says they are all gatekeepers now, which Carlkin treats as a larger responsibility handed down by deities or their equivalents. Asked after the missing companions, Sylan says the dragon is on a mission and another of them is at the pub.

plotSections.title: Gerk's mother and the blonde girl
bullets: Carlkin takes Sylan's papers, then leans down the stairs and asks whether Gerk's mother is dead. Gerk starts crying. Carlkin takes that as yes. Sylan calls it a soft subject and an orphan's situation. Carlkin says this is the first he has heard of it.

Carlkin says Gerk is probably seeing things. Gerk names a blonde girl with flowers and looks for the daisy in his hair. Carlkin calls it a hallucination. Asked whether Juten Prime knew, Sylan says she did not talk about it much; Plymouth Gawater was there when they told her. Carlkin claims he finally has something on them.

plotSections.title: A door to nowhere
bullets: The party admits a mishap on the flight: Gerk opened a doorway on the moving sky ship. Carlkin's first rule is not to open doors on moving things. A door stays where it was opened and bends time and space from wherever the opener is now. His second rule, framed as gatekeeping and being a Doorman, is not to open a door to a place you do not know, or the destination can be misread.

Gerk says he opened the lighthouse door with nowhere in mind. Carlkin says a door to nowhere opens into the nothing, the astral sea, or the space between arches. The creature almost used his living room as a birthing place. He calls it probably some kind of astral creature rather than simply an abomination. Gerk is glad it does not live there. If Gerk had been pulled through, a keystone and the party's mystical items could have gone with him into a hostile place, and Carlkin does not know what would have happened.

Gerk says nobody taught him the rules and he would not have taken the role if he had known the responsibilities. Carlkin says legend frames it as Gerk's own choice. Sylan says he investigated, concluded Gerk was the Doorman, and brought him that information because Gerk would not have found it alone, or not for a long time. Carlkin ties the role to the Mother's Prayer. He was present when Gerk learned to open doors, and Plymouth was there when Gerk received the power, but neither taught these rules. Carlkin will not name the scholars who study the Mother's Prayer. He calls it a conundrum, says Gerk is subject to the whims of the universe, and keeps some secrets in reserve: people underestimate what the old man in the crazy tower knows.

Sylan asks for the rules in writing. Carlkin doubts Gerk will read them. Sylan says he will work on it. Gerk says he cannot write, and Dana is sent for paper under a crate. Carlkin later lectures down through a knot in the floorboards and has Dana or Benji fetch paper. Gerk has been marking the floor; Carlkin tells him to stop. Gerk asks whether trees are dead. Sylan says the trees are living. Carlkin asks if Sylan's mother is a tree, and Sylan says it is complicated. Sylan hopes to bring his sister home.

plotSections.title: How a doorway is supposed to work
bullets: Carlkin says Gerk was told he can open doors and given a power-and-responsibility speech, but not how it works. The destination must be one exact door held clearly in mind, as if opening it by hand. His example is the front door of a particular longhouse, not a vague place-name, because many similar doors exist. Enough focus and familiarity connects the two places. A well-traveled Doorman could eventually open portals more freely, but portal magic is dangerous and should be kept simple.

Do not open a portal in a place you would want to sleep peacefully, and do not open one on a moving ship. The portal stays put while the ship moves, reality can tear, and a three-way opening can form. Bound to a keystone, Gerk will likely be asked to open portals related to that keystone. Carlkin says there are thirty keystones and that they connect the worlds. Once every keystone is seated together in one gate or gatehouse, the gatekeepers are more or less obligated to remain there, dormant, and keep the network safe.

Other people can open doors. The party has tried keystone portals and failed; only Gerk can open a door right now. Using a keystone does not strictly require being a doorman or gatekeeper. Long study is a workaround, and a key can be seated in a constructed gate that opens only to a predetermined place. A gatekeeper has more freedom: one opening can chain gatehouses. Opening toward a realm such as the Reach is not a single one-way door. Gatehouses sit on ley lines, and opening one functional gatehouse (his example is Midgar) also opens every other functional arch gatehouse at once, whether or not anyone is there. He corrects himself from eight other arches to seven. Away from a gatehouse, a keystone portal would still need a powerful ley-line crossing.

Carlkin will not call Gerk a doorman yet. Doormen were the prestigious rank and kept footmen as apprentices. Until Gerk earns the rank, Carlkin calls him a footman. He refuses to hold the rest of the conversation upstairs until Gerk promises no door will open in this place again. Gerk promises he never will. If Gerk announces he is about to open a door, Carlkin says he will teleport away and not be found.

plotSections.title: Carlkin's table and the lich emperor
bullets: Carlkin comes downstairs, sets out the good china, a real silver platter, and doilies, and pours a thin steaming tea-like drink from a jug like one Ord sometimes produces. He laces his own cup from a liquor bottle in a desk drawer. Cups are set for Dana, Gerk, Sylan, Ord (noted as technically present), Carlkin, and Benji. Benji has been watching the whole time and keeps relighting a pipe that sputters, sparks, and smells acrid. Carlkin asks them to explain what they need. They will make the agenda up as they go.

Sylan's first item: they are hunting a lich. Carlkin does not know the name Grixto. He does know the Emperor of Nyx. Sylan says they are the same person. The Emperor of the Hobgoblins was a lich who took Sylan's homeland and Nyx by shrewd, underhanded means. The party brought that emperor down, then learned he was a lich, killed him once without knowing what he was, and later found him again. They hunt him now because he wants the keystones.

Carlkin already knew the hobgoblins had fallen into civil war and that other peoples were afraid. He says he should have assumed this party was involved in destabilizing a continent, and that ending that regime was good. He concludes they killed the body and never destroyed the phylactery. Sylan says the phylactery stays on Grixto's person and is a small mundane item. Clues point to his fondness for chess and game pieces. He has been hard to find. Sylan believes they pilfered him at least once and did not find it. Carlkin calls him an overconfident lich who was betting they would not recognize what he was, and who has been playing them.

plotSections.title: The helmet and the phylactery
bullets: The party found nothing that looked like the phylactery. Carlkin walks them through it: a mundane item on the lich, a body that crumbled to dust, and a looting. Unless something like a notebook or diary was left behind, it is very likely still on someone in the party. A lich with millennia to plan could put the enchantment on an ordinary object and let them carry it.

Dana remembers that Walker took Grixto's helmet and still wears it as a style choice. She says it is the only thing he kept. Sylan calls that a bold place to hide a phylactery. They set the question aside until Walker is back.

Carlkin's shop has residual detect magic, indicated on a couple of bangles, that automatically notices magical items brought inside. It did not flag the party because something is masking their magical items, and it would not treat Gerk's door as a magical item. Asked whether the masking piece is complex or simple, Sylan pulls a necklace, rubs his neck, and says he believes it is simple.

plotSections.title: Contact since the second death
bullets: The lich has reached out twice since they vanquished him the second time, through the same kind of contact he used to control the hobgoblins. They answered. Dana thinks it was a spell, but she never got a dispel magic off, so she cannot confirm it. It was described to her as a fire that overtakes the mind, and she does not know how it works. She allows it may be a high-powered spell that only resembles that link.

Carlkin concludes a reply means he was sending sentences, so it is a Sending rather than a standing mental link, even if Grixto also has mental-link abilities and his power is beyond an ordinary sending. Carlkin is badly shaken by lich contact and abyss portals in his home on the same day, and says he could look the spells up.

On the latest contact the lich asked if they had found a better path. Dana reads his dealings as an attempt to consume them into his legion, not merely convert them, and answered that the path she had chosen was sufficient. Gerk talked through his day, his feelings, and a long account of his general well-being, which the lich did not like. Sylan said they were still looking and would find him. The lich had been pleased they had left him alone for a while.

plotSections.title: Garixto, Galixtar, and the Book of Vecna
bullets: Dana tells Carlkin the lich has the Book of Vecna, an extremely powerful spellbook and the source of his many spells. It is what he found when he stopped being a dragon rider and began hunting dragon riders. Carlkin is stunned. Benji says there is a lot to take in and asks whether this dragon rider was from The Reach. Dana confirms he was, and gives his original name as Garixto. Sylan names his dragon Galixtar, a red dragon.

Carlkin knows the legend from the late heyday of the dragon riders: Garixto the Betrayer and Galixtar, the Twin Bloody Comet. He places it long ago, corrects himself from thousands of years toward something on the order of hundreds or fifteen hundred, and says time on this arch is strange. Trainees were warned to be wary of anyone seeking their heart of hearts, and to give that only to the rider they are bonded with, and only when death is inevitable. Old dragons who lost their riders mourned that they had not given the heart over.

Carlkin remembers Galixtar as slain by the dragon rider Elrus, who was not yet legendary and was a trainer in that era. He does not remember whether Elrus was elf or human. Some say Elrus is still around. Dana says they have seen Galixtar, long dead, summoned in necrotic form and fought in Gilbrick. She does not know whether to call that form a ghost or a summon. Asked whether the legend is true that Garixto killed all his kin, Dana says that in the visions she has seen, he killed at least some of the young ones. Carlkin connects this lich to killing dragons and stealing Al Kurin, and asks where Walker and his dragon are.

plotSections.title: Nyx, Gilbrick, and the second killing
bullets: Carlkin recalls that the Nyx war ended in liberation, that some hobgoblins changed sides, and that a civil war followed. He asks how a man they had already killed was in Gilbrick. Dana says they killed Garixto once, and a second time after he had captured the Council of Nyx. The party searched for the captives, at one point suspecting Gilbrick, and traveled the arches there.
In Gilbrick they found Garixto, a keystone, and what Dana believes used to be a gatehouse. He summoned Galixtar's necrotic form. They vanquished him again there, and he has contacted them since.

plotSections.title: Walker finds Vecna waiting
bullets: Walker stands before Vecna, who sits semi-relaxed, tapping old game pieces on a table. Vecna has been waiting and greets him as someone looking for Vecna's book. Walker had sent Elrus in ahead; Elrus is scrambling down the passage, and Vecna takes the approaching figure for another of Walker's comrades.

Walker says Vecna is no nearer to finding Galixtar or the book. Vecna wants the red-skinned book back. He came because an elder showed the party a vision of the belongings' last known location. He offers the finder boons and says he does not patronize often, but he will make deals for those who do him a favor. Walker, out of character, treats a deal with Vecna as a very bad idea and does not want to be indebted. In character he brushes the offered favor off as something cheap he no longer wants, and Vecna offers other luxuries instead.

Gerk checks that they have the right person. This speaker is not Grixto: Grixto is the lich, and he and Galixtar are together. Of Galixtar, the guess is that she is an aberration, a possessed spirit tied to a piece.

plotSections.title: The unfinished bargain
bullets: Walker says he is not after the book. He is after Grixto, and he says Grixto and Galixtar are together. He wants the phylactery and does not know what it is. Vecna wants a book he wrote, which the lich allegedly has. Walker remembers the vision as coming from Emhet. Vecna says it showed a very young, adolescent upstart lich fresh from his change, with the book clearly visible, including its name and appearance.

Walker proposes they might help each other. Vecna first hears an exchange of locations. Walker revises it: if Walker comes to hold the book and Vecna comes to hold the phylactery, they could trade. Dana rejects that trade. Vecna restates it as him recovering the phylactery, the party recovering the book, and then an exchange. Walker says that is not the deal, only that if each ends up holding what the other wants, it could be a business opportunity. He asks for a way to contact Vecna, such as a carrier pigeon or a sending. Vecna agrees he can make an arrangement: if he finds the location or the object, he will send Walker, and that would be the deal.

Vecna calls the bargain one-sided. He would be giving the phylactery's identity and its location, while Walker would only return a book Walker already knows by sight, so Vecna says he deserves more than the book. Walker warns him not to name the phylactery in a way that would put Walker in his debt. Hypothetically, Vecna could name the Raskina as the phylactery and call his side fulfilled, and Walker would then have to procure it. Walker says that if the Raskina is the phylactery he will destroy it, which would void the bargain. He does not close the deal. He will think it over while he keeps searching the room, including under the chair, and Vecna watches from the chair.

Someone who overheard warns that dealing with a demigod of the undead seems unwise. They say Vecna may be why their order fell, if his book led to that, and ask whether the party should seek whatever darkness is in the book no matter what Vecna could give them. Walker calls that a fair point, then questions Vecna outside the deal, while still valuing his resources.

plotSections.title: Vecna's origin and the book
bullets: Asked why he wants the book, Vecna says he wrote it. It has legacy and story, and like him it requires grandeur. He says he was not originally a god and is denoted a demigod rather than a full or Voyager god; he treats the difference as semantics and a matter of followers. He was born in Atlas among the first peoples, is not of the Navi line, and was not born in this room or this plane. He claims an interest in keeping Atlas as it should be. Voyager gods came from other pantheons, brought in by other creatures like vermin on ships. He says he is not an elder.

He describes himself as a farmer's bastard whose father died before he could claim land. He was poor, no fighter, and became a plotter who stole and read, in that way similar to Grixto. The 'deep, dark' origin is framing; he says the place really was neither. What sets them apart, he says, is that Grixto does not appear to have had a sister.

His sister's name was Valkyrie. He says the name has been watered down until people no longer recognize the legend, that she was courageous, and that she may have been one of the first shield maidens. He claims he knew the seed of that legend. Walker only knows the pop-culture sense of a warrior-angel woman. She supported his reading and did the labor he could not. There is no happy ending: he killed her, skinned her half alive, and used her blood as the ink. He cast the runes; he did not write the pages. The void torn in the family made the book write itself. He says demons write in it and that he gained knowledge from them. Recovering it would be a family reunion. Walker argues that if Vecna is not the author he is only a product of the book. Vecna rejects that: he cast the runes and used what he gained, so the book is his, and he still needs it because its contents are not only what he already knew. The cover is understood to be that long-dead sister's skin.

plotSections.title: Lichdom, faith, and domains
bullets: Walker asks whether Vecna is a lich as well as a demigod. Vecna says he began as a lich and has transcended that. Enough followers matter: even when magic fails, the faith of a few peasants can outdo years of study. Asked how to gain followers, he first jokes about killing a sister. Walker says his family is all dead.

Followers alone do not make a god. Kings, kind or cruel, stay fleeting, and the fey do not do what transcendence requires. A domain is also required, usually stolen from whoever held it last, and the other gods can block a bid. Access to souls is another requirement. Vecna's domains are the undead and secrets, not death itself. Orcus, a demon prince, has an overlapping claim on the undead.

He points Sylan at domain-stealing and explains the Raven Queen's failed reach for the throne of complete undeath. The other gods stopped her. She holds death, the vague moment between, not undeath. Undead are not sent back through death; they are returned to where they were, so she gets no claim on them, and they would otherwise pass through her domain again. Vecna jokes that Walker might use the lesson, and the book, to become a malevolent god of the undead and take his throne. Walker refuses. Vecna adds that a gathering of gods gets little done, which he says the party already knows.

plotSections.title: The field book
bullets: Walker says he came to work out Grixto and the phylactery and is still missing something. Vecna points him at the book and says it is worth ruling out as the phylactery. Walker is sure it is not, and Vecna agrees. Vecna says the book can heal an itch, work as a seeking tool to find the phylactery, and bring back lost people, things, or beings. He calls life and death two sides of the same coin. Walker refuses any path that would mean killing someone's sister and stops him when restoration of the lost comes up. Vecna says he has already done that.

Walker leaves a later trade open but unmade: what he learns about the book for what Vecna learns about the phylactery. He has nothing to trade yet and apologizes for coming empty-handed. Vecna says the visit was not a waste and that he enjoys the company.

Vecna conjures a miniature of the Raskina from Walker's vision, a field-notes copy about a foot square, detailed enough that the pages feel as if they would crinkle. The cover looks like black leather but is not any leather Walker knows, and is taken to be his sister's skin. With it is a small bright-red quill and no inkwell. The quill is semi-warm. The stated use is communication: write in the book and Vecna will answer. Walker asks if there is any other catch and is told no. He shudders and takes the book and quill anyway.

plotSections.title: The roost cave
bullets: Elrus stays silent through the talk, sword at his belt, staring Vecna down. Walker then asks him to help search. Walker's Investigation is 11. Nothing in the room is identified as the phylactery.

The cave matches Walker's vision and has a roost side and a study side. The roost has no bedding, only a thin layer of dirt, weeds in the light from the entrance, fungi, and bat guano. The study has a square slab table where Vecna sits. It once held maps and now has only faint papery scraps; Walker cannot tell whether they are aged paper or something skin-like. Three chairs, each hewn from one piece of lighter stone, and old troop markers on the ground and table are the other contents.

The back wall, continuing into the roost, carries four rudimentary landscape carvings, one for each cardinal direction. They are local views Walker half-recognizes from the top of the training yard and from the old tower at the center of the stronghold. They do not read as writing. Each is slightly tilted, as if drawn from memory after standing on that tower. Elrus gives the mismatch as about ten degrees one way and about twenty-five degrees the other. He thinks Grixto committed the views to memory and carved them later with the angles off, but he cannot reconcile that with one vantage: it is as if Grixto had shifted location while still standing in the same spot. The tower itself is already rubble, seen on the way in. Walker asks to be taken there and says he has an idea. Vecna is still seated and watching.

plotSections.title: Leaving Vecna
bullets: Elrus asks what to do about Vecna and whether Walker is about to make a deal. He calls the sister story morbid. The party chooses not to make a deal. Walker says to ignore him and that less contact is better, then on the way out nods and wishes him luck finding the sister-skin book.

Vecna wishes them luck in return and asks if there is a deal. Walker says not right now, and that he knows how to find him. Vecna tells him to write in the book when he is ready. Walker keeps the courtesy up in the room, polite but slightly irreverent, because he thinks showing only fear would lose Vecna's respect. Once out of sight he admits Vecna frightens him and drops the act.

plotSections.title: The guild ruins and Walker's theory
bullets: Elrus leads them up the winding half-path out of the cavern. Glimmen backtracks and meets Walker and Elrus on the plains, then they make a short jump to the cliffside ruins of the guild stronghold from Elrus and Grixto's past. It was an average stronghold, with larger footprints for housing dragons, a huge stable cut into the cliff and joined by a covered walkway that is now only scattered tiles and an overgrown footprint, and a central tower whose standing walls are about five or six feet high. The tower's footprint is about eighty feet across. Moss, grass, vines, bushes, and trees have taken the ruins.

Walker recalls Elrus's warning that if a dragon or its rider dies, the other most often goes mad. Elrus confirms that. Asked whether that madness would be enough to send someone after a book that could bring the other back, Elrus says yes: in that state he would abandon reason.

Walker's theory, formed while Vecna was talking, is that Galixtar was already dead before Grixto became a lich, and that restoring her is why he wanted lichdom and the Al Kurin. Elrus treats this as a real motivation. Galixtar did not seem different at the time, but the new magic might have kept her from presenting as undead, and the party's vision is from years later. He says the theory also explains Grixto's eagerness for the Al Kurin and makes more sense than most explanations he has heard, while still sounding unsure it would by itself drive a mind that far.

plotSections.title: The tilted landmarks
bullets: From about eighty feet up, where the tower used to stand, the party can see the same east, west, north, and south landmarks that were carved on the cave wall. Elrus's tilt is a bearing error, not a leaning mountain. Each major landmark, usually the largest mountain or island on that side, sits slightly off the cardinal direction it should occupy. On the wall, the western landmark was drawn as if a clock's hour hand had moved from nine o'clock toward nine-twenty or nine-thirty.

Walker reads the offset as a clue. He wants to rotate until the real landmarks match the cave drawings, then look along that facing for a destination or hint. He calls for an investigation check. The result is not yet in.

log: The fight's noise wakes Benji in the lighthouse base, where he gets up from a pile of old memorabilia. Carlkin has already run upstairs.
Gerk fails to re-level the broken cobbles (Sleight of Hand 4), leaving the hole through the floor. Carlkin tells him to stop.
The closed door is gone, with no lasting trace except the damaged floor. Sylan confirms that and calls up that the lower level should be safe.

Carlkin reacts with alarm that they are opening doors in his lighthouse without knowing how. He forbids more portals, starts a house rule against them, and demands his paper and good pen. Sylan is upstairs with him; Gerk is still at the floor; Dana has not moved.
Sylan brings the quill and ink. He says the party holds the keystones again after finishing the delivery to Juten Prime, because of a prophecy centered on Gerk.

Benji watches from a crate, packs, and lights a copper corncob pipe. Carlkin takes the pages Sylan gave him, packs and lights a grass-like pipe with a drop of oil, and starts writing as sulfurous, earthy smoke fills the room.
Carlkin leans down the stairs and asks if Gerk's mother is dead. Gerk cries at once. Carlkin treats that as a yes and they treat Gerk as an orphan. Sylan says the subject is sensitive.
Gerk describes a blonde girl with flowers and searches his hair for a daisy. Carlkin calls it a hallucination.
Sylan says Juten Prime barely discussed it, and that Plymouth Gawater was present when they explained it. Carlkin claims he now has an edge on them.
Carlkin scolds Gerk for opening doors. The party confirms the mishap happened on a moving sky ship. Gerk says Plymouth was present when he gained the ability.

Sylan explains that he uncovered Gerk's role as the Doorman and told him. Carlkin connects that role to the Mother's Prayer, says it would eventually have been involved, and notes that Plymouth taught the power without the rules. Sylan offers to record the rules for Gerk.

Carlkin gives the first Doorman rule: never open a doorway on something that is moving, because the doorway stays put and bends time and space from where the opener is. Gerk's ship doorway stayed fixed while the ship moved.

Carlkin checks who is absent and whether everyone holds a keystone. Sylan confirms four keystones are here. The dragon is on a mission and another companion is at the pub. Dana says they are all gatekeepers.

Second rule: do not open a door to an unknown place. Gerk says he aimed the door at nowhere and had no destination. Carlkin identifies that as a door between the arches, into the nothing or the astral sea, and says the astral creature nearly used the room to be born. He calls it an astral creature rather than an abomination.
Carlkin says he does not know what would have happened if Gerk and a keystone, along with the party's mystical items, had been pulled through, and that ignorance is why it must not be tested.
Gerk mimes opening a door. Carlkin flees upstairs and continues through a knothole in the floor. He tells Gerk to leave the floor; Mending will repair it later.

Speaking through the floorboards, Carlkin teaches safe targeting: one specific, familiar door visualized as if opened by hand. He forbids portals on moving ships and in places meant for peaceful rest, and warns that a portal can stay fixed, tear reality, and become a three-way opening.
Carlkin says the Mother's Prayer is a studied conundrum. He refuses to name the scholars and keeps some secrets because people underestimate the man in the tower.
Sylan says the trees are alive and, asked if his mother is a tree, answers that it is complicated. He asks whether a keystone requires a Doorman or a guardian.

Carlkin explains thirty keystones and gatehouses on ley lines. Keystone use is generally for a gatekeeper or doorman. A seated key can open a fixed, predetermined gate. A gatekeeper can chain every functional ley-line gatehouse at once; he corrects the count to seven other arches. Opening one functional arch gatehouse opens the other functional ones at once.

A keystone-bound Doorman will be asked for portals tied to that stone. Assembling every keystone in one gatehouse would pin the gatekeepers there as dormant guardians. Only study, or a keyed gate fixed to one destination, bypasses needing a gatekeeper or doorman. Carlkin confirms other people can open doors, then will not discuss the other doormen.

Sylan says only Gerk can open a door so far, and that he hopes bringing his sister home will matter. Carlkin moves the talk downstairs, gets Gerk's promise never to open a door here again, names him footman rather than doorman, and threatens to teleport away for good if another door opens.
Carlkin serves the good china and a tea-like drink, spiked for himself, to Dana, Gerk, Sylan, Ord, Benji, and himself, and asks what they need. Benji watches and smokes.

Sylan identifies Grixto as the Emperor of Nyx and of the hobgoblins, a lich who seized Sylan's homeland and Nyx, was killed once, returned, and is hunting the keystones. The phylactery is a small mundane item kept on him, possibly among chess or game pieces. A prior looting did not find it.

Carlkin presses them: they killed the lich, decided the phylactery was a mundane item on his person, and did not identify it among what he carried. He recounts a continental conquest, a death in front of them, and a mask put on as they learned he was a lich, and asks whether they investigated.

Dana remembers that Walker took the lich's helmet and still wears it as a style choice. Carlkin asks what else of the lich's they are wearing. Dana says the helmet is the only thing Walker kept. Sylan says the lich crumbled to dust when they cut him down.

Carlkin explains the shop's residual detect magic. Their items did not flag because something is masking the party's magic. Sylan shows a simple necklace. Carlkin says a simple item is exactly what a lich could turn into a hidden phylactery, warns that they have likely been carrying it, and that it may be on the party now. They postpone the check until Walker returns.

Carlkin asks whether the lich sought them out. Dana says Grixto has contacted them twice since the second defeat, through the same kind of mental link he used on the hobgoblins. She thinks it was a spell, they replied, she never dispelled it, and she cannot confirm spell versus link. She describes a fire overtaking the mind. Carlkin reads the reply as a Sending. Dana says the lich's interactions are an attempt to consume them.

Sylan says Grixto has an extremely powerful spellbook and access to many spells. Dana names it the Book of Vecna, found when Grixto turned from dragon rider to hunter of dragon riders. Carlkin is speechless.

Benji says it is a lot to take in, confirms the man was a dragon rider, and asks if he is from The Reach. Dana says yes, and that his original name was Garixto. Sylan names the dragon Galixtar, a red dragon.

Carlkin recounts the legend of Galixtar, killed by the dragon rider Elrus, and of Garixto the Betrayer and Galixtar as the Twin Bloody Comet, including the warning about the heart of hearts. The party confirms the lich is Garixto and that they have seen Galixtar.

Dana says Grixto can summon Galixtar and that they fought her summoned, necrotic form in Gilbrick. They do not know if she is a ghost or a summon. Carlkin, badly shaken, asks how the lich was there if they had already killed him.

Dana explains the timeline: they killed Garixto once while he held the Council of Nyx; searching the arches led them to Gilbrick, a keystone, and a former gatehouse, where they killed him again after he summoned Galixtar. He has contacted them since.

Carlkin asks what they told the lich. Grixto had asked if they had found a better path. Dana answered that her chosen path was sufficient, taking the offer as a call to rejoin his legion. Gerk buried him in a long account of his day, his feelings, and his well-being, which the lich disliked. Sylan told him they were still looking and would find him, after the lich had been glad to be left alone.

Carlkin asks if Garixto killed all of his kin. Dana's visions show he killed at least some of the young ones, not necessarily all. The question then turns to where Walker and his dragon are if the lich is killing dragons and stealing Al Kurin.

The scene is Walker before Vecna, who is waiting at a table with old game pieces and looking for his book. Elrus, sent by Walker, scrambles down the passage. Walker says Vecna is no nearer to Galixtar or the red-skinned book. Vecna says an elder's vision of the book's last known location brought him here, and he offers boons or a deal to whoever finds it.

Walker says he wants Grixto, and that Grixto and Galixtar are together. Gerk confirms they are speaking to the intended person. Vecna says this is not Grixto: Grixto is the lich and is paired with Galixtar, whom Vecna guesses is an aberration, a possessed spirit tied to a piece.

Walker proposes they can help each other: he wants the lich's phylactery, and Vecna wants a book the lich allegedly has. Vecna first treats it as a location swap, then as each retrieving the other's object. Dana objects. Walker narrows it to a possible later exchange if each holds what the other wants.

Vecna asks whether Walker knows what the phylactery is. Walker says no, and that it is bold to assume he knows what the book looks like; he only has suspicions. Vecna says the deal is uneven, because he would be supplying both the phylactery's location and its identity, and he wants more than the return of the book.
Vecna says Walker already saw the book, and its name, in the vision from Emhet: a young adolescent lich, a sprite-like upstart fresh from his change, with the book clearly visible.

Walker asks for a way to contact Vecna, such as a messenger, a carrier pigeon, or a sending. Vecna agrees to make an arrangement and offers to even the deal: if he finds the phylactery's location or the object, he will send word.

Vecna hypothesizes that naming the Raskina as the phylactery would fulfill his side, and Walker would then have to bring it to him. He dares the lich to try hiding a phylactery that way. Walker says that if the Raskina is the phylactery he must destroy it, voiding the deal.

A listener who overheard warns that a deal with a demigod of the undead seems unwise, because Vecna's book may be why their order fell, and questions whether that book should be found at all. Walker agrees it is a fair point.
Walker says the next questions are not part of the deal and asks why Vecna wants the book. Vecna says he wrote it, that it carries legacy and story, and that it requires grandeur.

Vecna says he is a demigod born in Atlas, not an elder and not one of the voyager gods brought from other pantheons, and that he is invested in Atlas remaining as it should be. He distinguishes himself from the Navi and tells an origin as a landless farmer's bastard who survived by plotting, theft, and reading rather than fighting. He likens that life to Grixto's and says Grixto seems to have had no sister.

Vecna names his sister Valkyrie, ties her to the shield-maiden legend, and says he killed and skinned her, bound the book in her skin, and used her blood as ink. The book wrote itself after he tore a void in the family, with demons writing in it. He still needs it and calls that a family reunion. Walker asks why he still needs a book he caused to exist. Vecna says he cast the runes and drew power from knowledge the demons provided.

Walker asks whether Vecna is a witch and a lich. Vecna says he began as a lich and has transcended that through faith and followers. Asked how one gets followers, Vecna jokes about killing a sister. Walker says all his family is dead.

Vecna explains that kings and the fey do not transcend: followers are only one step, and a domain and access to souls are also required. He names his domains as the undead and secrets, with an overlap claimed by the Demon Prince Orcus. Other gods blocked the Raven Queen from undeath: she received death, the moment between, but not the undead, because the undead are returned to where they were found instead of passing through death.

Walker says he came for Grixto's phylactery and is missing something. Vecna indicates his book. Walker is certain the book is not the phylactery. Vecna says the book can seek the phylactery, ease an itch, and restore lost people, things, or beings. Walker presses him to repeat the restoration claim and says he will not kill someone's sister to use it. Vecna says he already killed her.
Walker proposes a future exchange of book-knowledge for phylactery-knowledge and apologizes for coming empty-handed. Vecna dismisses the apology and says he enjoys the company.

Vecna produces a miniature Raskina field book bound in what is taken to be his long-dead sister's skin, plus a warm red quill and no inkwell. Writing in the book is how Walker can reach him. Walker takes both. Elrus has watched the whole exchange in silence, hand on his sword.

Walker postpones the deal and searches with Elrus (Investigation 11). Vecna remains seated and observing; Walker asks him to move so he can look under the chair. The roost is bare dirt, weeds, fungi, and bat guano. The study holds a slab table, papery scraps, three light stone chairs, and old troop markers. Four cardinal landscape carvings show views from the old central tower, all slightly tilted. There is no phylactery.

Elrus reads the carvings as cardinal views from the old central tower, drawn from memory by Grixto and several degrees off. He recognizes the local mountains and cannot explain the tilt. Walker confirms Vecna is still there, learns the tower is rubble, and asks to be taken to it.

Walker refuses a deal for now, tells the others to leave Vecna alone, and wishes him luck finding the sister-skin book. Vecna says to write him a letter in his book when they are ready. The party leaves the cavern.
Elrus leads them up to the plains, where Glimmen rejoins them, and then to the cliffside ruins of Elrus and Grixto's old guild stronghold.

Elrus confirms that a dragon or rider who loses the other most often goes mad, and that such madness could drive a search for a book to bring the other back. Walker proposes that Galixtar died before Grixto became a lich, which would explain both the lichdom and the hunt for the Al Kurin. Elrus calls it a plausible motive and a better theory than most he has heard.
From the old tower's height, Elrus shows that the cardinal landmarks are drawn a few degrees off true. Walker tries to use that tilt as a direction clue and begins an investigation check.
